display_title: Official Review of Paper3590 by Reviewer 1itH

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the deep neural network compression problem. Different from previous works that are either restricted to the underlying network operations without changing the architecture, or involving significant domain knowledge or manual design via knowledge distillation for architeture changes, this paper proposes to conduct knowledge distillation on operation level. The proposed method automatically replaces inefficient operations in a given network with more efficient counterparts. The underlying problem is reformulated as a search problem. Seen from the results, the proposed method works well.
content.main_review: The major concern might be the "hardware aware" in the title. To the reviewer, one compression method is called hardware aware if it can easily adapt to a new specific hardware w.r.t. latency, memory, storage size on disk. Basically, the hardware aware method should not be fixed with any single artificial measure. For example, storage size does not necessarily be linear with the parameter counts, as it depends on how the parameters of a model are indexed and stored on the disk. For this method, the neural archtecture is searched by selecting operations with minimal latency. The latency of the operations are however precomputed on a specific hardware and form a latency look-up table. On one hand, such mechansim simply restricts the compression method only "aware" to latency, as the memory and storage size of the whole model may not be naively additive to each operation. On the other hand, precomputing the latency of each operation can involve considerable noise especially when the hardware is conducting multi-tasks (e.g., CPU), making the later operation selection phase inaccurate. Besides, how complex and difficult it is to precompute the latency lookup table on any new hardware? Also, it is suggested to modify the titile as "latency aware", as the proposed method does not adapt to memery, storage and other hardware measures.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The contribution of this paper is clear, despite the "hardware" in title is not accurate.
The technique design seems correct and the empirical results support it well.
The writting is relatively smooth.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3590 by Reviewer 1itH

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for the feedback and great suggestions.

**Hardware-aware -> Latency-aware.** We agree that the real latency depends on scheduling, memory access and interference from other processes. Therefore, we can only target relative latency reduction. Our method can be applied to reduce memory, flops or parameters by changing the cost vector $b$. We agree that our results only support latency reduction and we will rename the paper to “Latency aware network acceleration”. 

Computing LUT for EfficientNetV1-B2 has a one-time cost of <30 minutes on the device for Jetson Nano and even less for more powerful devices. To create a LUT, we fetch the dimensions of input and output tensors for every layer and measure the speed of all operations under this restriction. Therefore, every operation is measured for every layer. We keep the load to be minimal on the device. We repeat measurement of every operator 10 times; if the number is increased to 100, the cost of getting the lookup table will be 10x more.

We are happy to provide more details and we agree to change the title. We appreciate it if you could let us know if we could address your comments and if you could reconsider your rating.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3590 by Reviewer 45NN

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to transform a pretrained neural network to meet latency constraints on target hardware by replacing inefficient operations with efficient ones. For this, this method conducts knowledge distillation from the layers of the given neural network to candidate operations. Then, it formulates the search problem as a linear integer optimization to search for the best architectures. To demonstrate such a method, EfficientNetV1, EfficientNetV2, and ResNetST are used as a target network and GPU and CPU are used as target devices.
content.main_review:
Strength

- This paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- The reviewer thinks the proposed approach is novel and interesting. To my knowledge, this work is the first work to propose layer-wise knowledge distillation as a pretraining stage for network transformation.
- This method is flexible to design search space since adding or subtracting candidate operations without retraining all operations of search space while existing supernet-based NAS methods need to re-train all operations.

Weakness

[Major]

- When I first read the goal of this work such that "transforming/replacing" neural networks for improving efficiency, I expected that, on a target task, rapid process time and a simple pipeline for practical usage compared with existing NAS works that start from scratch. However, in Table 1, this work has longer times (100eL) compared with existing works (75eL - Once-For-All, 50eL - DONNA).
    - Furthermore, assume that we have EfficientNetV1-B0 as the base network, EfficientNet-like approaches can rapidly get transformed network fitting on latency constraints by simply scaling. Compared with this, this work requires too much time to transform the base network. Considering this and the large fine-tuning cost, the reviewer thinks the performance is not that impressive.
- This work covers a large search space ($O(10^{100})$ compared with existing works. Yet, there seems to be a lack of theoretical analysis or empirical experiments to support the advantage of considering the large search space. To my knowledge, recently, many works[1,2] have been shown that we do not need to use large search space since focusing on valid operations or architectures on the smaller search space is enough for the NAS process.
    - Additionally, this work included layers of Transformer in the architecture candidate set and argues that this is one of their main contributions. Yet, if I read correctly, I did not see in which cases it helps to obtain better-performing architectures.
- Even though this work focuses on hardware-aware, the number of target devices is two (GPU and CPU).  Once-for-all that one of comparison of this work handled 5 various device platforms (GPU/CPU/Mobile/Edge GPU/FPGA) and more number of devices dependent on the manufacturer (e.g. Google/Samsung/LG). the reviewer thinks this work needs to demonstrate the generality of the proposed method on various devices.

[Minor]

- I wonder about the number of parameters and FLOPS information of models and the reason why the resolution of input images are different per models in Table 2.
- The measure (e.g. Spearman or Kendal Tau) looks missing in the sentence "Note that our LUT-based latency estimation has ~0.99 correlation with ~".
- The definition of $\mathcal{S}$ looks missing and that of $X_{tr}$ in equation (1) looks missing.

[1] Compound Once-For-All Networks for Faster Multi-Platform Deployment, ICLR2021.
 
[2] On network design spaces for visual recognition. CVPR 2019
content.summary_of_the_review:
The reviewer thinks the main approach that layer-wise knowledge distillation for hardware-aware network transformation is novel and interesting. Yet, the contributions for the NAS field are rather weak to accept the paper: 
1) the total time cost of this method is larger than existing NAS methods (Once-For-All, DONNA, and EfficientNet series) and considering large fine-tuning cost, the performance is not impressive.
2) Lack of theoretical analysis or empirical experiments to demonstrate the advantage of the large search space, which is one of the main contributions.
3) Lack of generality on many types of hardwares.

content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing the paper and providing detailed comments. Please see our rebuttal on the raised issues.

> 1. When I first read the goal of this work such that "transforming/replacing" neural networks for improving efficiency, I expected that, on a target task, rapid process time and a simple pipeline for practical usage compared with existing NAS works that start from scratch. However, in Table 1, this work has longer times (100eL) compared with existing works (75eL - Once-For-All, 50eL - DONNA).

Probably there is a misunderstanding: the total cost obtaining L models with different computational budgets is listed as Total cost, HANT is significantly faster and more resource-efficient than others. The length of finetuning by itself doesn’t contribute to the original idea. It has a minor effect on the total cost as shown in Table 1. Additionally, our approach supports zero-shot teacher-student NAS as described in the original paper, page 8, section `Zero-shot HANT.` In this case, the initialization costs are neglectable.

Reducing finetuning to 50 or even 25 epochs still produces reasonable models that are better than vanilla EfficientNetsV1-B0/B1 trained from scratch as we can see below: 

| Model      |    25       |    50       | 100      |  vanilla EficientNet |
|:---------|:----------:|:---------:|:---------:|----------------------:|
| 0.45xB2   |   79.19  |    79.58  |  79.71  |   EficientNetV1-B0 (77.70) |
| 0.55xB2   |   79.84    |    80.00    | 80.11   |  EficientNetV1-B1 (78.83) |

Please let us know if the issue with the finetuning cost is addressed. 

> Furthermore, assume that we have EfficientNetV1-B0 as the base network, EfficientNet-like approaches can rapidly get transformed network fitting on latency constraints by simply scaling. Compared with this, this work requires too much time to transform the base network. Considering this and the large fine-tuning cost, the reviewer thinks the performance is not that impressive.

In Table 2, we present results where models compressed by HANT are significantly better (up to 3% improvement) than vanilla EfficientNet scaling for all models/experiments. For example, compressing EfficientNetB4 by 4x we gain 3% over the vanilla B1 model. Moreover, the EfficientNet scaling mechanism requires training models from scratch for 350 epochs for every new variant, our full approach will be more efficient if at least 2 models are required (original teacher training is 350 epochs and a derivative model will require a cost of 197 epochs at once and 100e for every derivative, so 2 models the cost is 647, for 3 - 747; In original EfficientNet, to get 2 models the cost is 700 epochs, 3 translates to 1050). The difference grows when more models are required. Concluding, the training cost is reduced and better results are obtained with HANT over vanilla EfficientNetV1 scaling.    

> This work covers a large search space ($O(10^100)$ compared with existing works. Yet, there seems to be a lack of theoretical analysis or empirical experiments to support the advantage of considering the large search space. To my knowledge, recently, many works[1,2] have been shown that we do not need to use large search space since focusing on valid operations or architectures on the smaller search space is enough for the NAS process.

**On the large search space.** Large search space is needed when the set of optimal operators is not known a priori and the depth of the model should be adjusted automatically. If the user knows (we didn’t beforehand) that transformers will not be efficient to replace CNN layers then they can be removed, same for other operators as well to reduce the search space. But even in that case running other NAS approaches will be very costly, see Table 1, OFA method. Working on a larger space is a feature of our approach that is only possible with our ILP formulation. HANT is a way to analyze a large search space to obtain insights for building better models, please section `3.2.1 architecture insights` page 9. We automatically found modifications to EfficeintNetV1 that allow us to outperform EfficientNetV2.

To verify the benefit of a larger search space, we conducted experiments with a restricted search space. For that we randomly pick 5/10 operations from every layer to participate in ILP; results are averaged over 5 runs. We also add results from the Zero-shot experiment (2 ops) presented in the original paper:

| Model                |    2 ops (zero-shot)       |    5 operations  |  10 operations     | All      |
|:-------------------|:-------------------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:------------:|
| 0.55xEfficientNet V1-B2   |    79.40   |      79.52    |  79.66    | 80.00   |

The original model has an accuracy of 80.07, finetuning for 50 epochs. We observe that accuracy improves as the search space becomes larger.

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing the paper. Please see below our answers to the posted weaknesses:  

> 1. The novelty of this paper is a bit weak. The proposed framework is very similar to NAS. In addition, the usage of layer-wise knowledge distillation is straightforward. Similar explorations have been done in NAS (e.g., [1]).

**Knowledge distillation**. We do not claim that knowledge distillation is one of our novelties. However, we are the first who applied it in a layer-wise manner to enable search over a large space of operations and the depth of the module while allowing different operators inside the block. Prior work had difficulty with this because doing so results in a significantly larger search space, and traditional non-linear NAS approaches have a hard time with such optimization complexity. We talk about these aspects in the Related work section. 

The main novelty of the paper is in the relaxation of teacher-based NAS to the linear problem. This paper is the first to propose Integer Linear Programming as an architecture search method for accelerating an existing network. In the teacher-student setup, our method finds architectures constrained to the specified budget in a few seconds to minutes. The pretraining and scoring steps are done only once, and all models with various computational budgets are obtained extremely fast without consideration of the finetuning cost.  We even compare our method to two popular approaches of NAS: Gumbel-Max optimization and RL in Table 4. Finally, our method can search much faster than any other approach by a Zero shot formulation, see paragraph `Zero-shot HANT.` page 8 where no pretraining is required (pretraining cost is 0), and the search cost is neglectable, reducing the total cost to only finetuning (100 epochs).

**The work [1]** mentioned by the reviewer is already cited and compared in our original paper (see related work section). Please check the discussions on `DNA` or `Li et al. (2020)`, mentioned on page 3, paragraph 3, of the original paper. Detailed costs are compared in Table 1 emphasizes the difference by looking at the costs of different stages. HANT uses 1.6x less initialization cost, significantly (at least 14x faster) during the search phase, and is 4.5x faster in the finetuning.

> 1. In addition to GPU and cloud CPU, it would be interesting and useful to see the results of HANT on mobile phones. 

Our method will work with any hardware as long as we can get a reliable latency lookup table. Following the suggestion, we will add Nvidia Jetson Nano results to the paper. Note that this can be done easily using the existing pretrained operators from the paper, and by only searching and finetuning. We will also rename the paper to Latency Aware Network Acceleration to reduce the emphasis on the hardware claim.

Accuracy of the models optimized for a mobile edge device Jetson Nano, 50 epochs for finetuning:

|Model	| Optimized for Nano	| Accuracy | Latency, bs 32, ms |
|:----------|:--------------------------:|:------------:|------------------:|
| EfficientNetV1-B2          |                                               |  80.07       |       2206 ms |
|0.55xEfficientNetV1-B2	| +                                            | 79.38	    |      1265 ms  |
|0.45xEfficientNetV1-B2	| +                                            | 78.67	    |      1040 ms  |

Any suggestion on how to improve the paper will be very helpful. We believe that the topics in neural network acceleration such as pruning and NAS are of strong interest to the ICLR community.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper propose a hardware-aware network transformation method by combining the knowledge distillation method and constrained integer programming. The knowledge distillation is used for the initialization of the transformed networks, and the integer programming is for the acceleration of the searching process for the combination of candidate operations. Extensive experimental results show the efficacy of the method.
content.main_review:
Strengths: While there are more than 100 candidate operators for each layer, the knowledge distillation procedure only takes one epoch to converge, which saves time. What's more, by relaxing the searching problem, the integer programming is introduced, which greatly reduced the search time. The results on Efficientnet and ResNeSt show better accuracy and similar latency level.

Weaknesses: 
1. The main comparison in Table 2, which is also the main results of the paper, is not under aligned conditions. For example, why don't the authors compare the EfficientB2 with the 0.45xEfficientB2? If compared this way, it seems that there is a large accuracy degradation. 
2. the knowledge distillation process is used for each layer separately, without considering the relation between layers. Ablation study is desired to show the advantages or disadvantages of this separate knowledge distillation.

Reasons to accept:
1. The relaxation of the problem and the integer programming greatly reduce the search time for the second stage.
2. The empirical study is fair.

Reasons to reject: 
1. The comparisons in Table 2 is unfair. If we instead compare between models of the same family, no good results are obtained. For example, 0.55xEfficientB2 performs worse than the original EfficientB2. This result does not match the main idea of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper addresses the important problem of Neural Network Acceleration via approximation. The two stage construction of the proposed method, and the techniques used therein, are well founded. However, the empirical results are not that convincing and should be improved.

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
> 1. The main comparison in Table 2, which is also the main results of the paper, is not under aligned conditions. For example, why don't the authors compare the EfficientB2 with the 0.45xEfficientB2? If compared this way, it seems that there is a large accuracy degradation. 

Answer: After reviewing the reported numbers, we found that the accuracy of the original model was incorrect. We use the teacher network `tf_efficientnet_b2` from `timm` package. The accuracy of this model is 80.07. Therefore, our 0.55xB2 even outperforms the original model by 0.04%. Original accuracy can be verified at https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models/blob/master/results/results-imagenet.csv#L269, thank you for pointing this out!

The reported results in the table are grouped by the model latency (sections are organized by TRT latency (first <20ms, second <35ms, third <50ms, etc.)  In this way, we want to emphasize the accuracy gains of HANT when compared to faster models trained from scratch (EfficientNet scaling).   

We think that the reviewer missed other important empirical results:

- For all considered models we achieve 0.18-3.0% accuracy improvement when compressing larger models to the level of smaller (see EfficientNets B2->B0, B4->B2, etc). Table 2:
    - EfficientNetV1-B2 compressed to the level of EfficientNetV1-B0 achieves 2% accuracy improvement. Corresponds to 0.45xB2 in Table 2.
    - EfficientNetV1-B4 compressed to the level of EfficientNetV1-B1 achieves 3% improvement. Marked as 0.25xB4.
    - EfficientNetV1-B4 compressed to the level of EfficientNetV1-B2 achieves 2.1% improvement. Marked as 0.3xB4.
    - EfficientNetV2-B3 compressed to the level of EfficientNetV1-B2 achieves 0.93% improvement. Marked as 0.6xB3 under EfficientNetV2 section.
- HANT achieves significant real speed-ups with little to no accuracy drop (Table 2): 
    - EfficeintNetB6 accelerated by 3.6x and 1.8x times by trading-off 0.34% and 0.11% accuracy, respectively. 
    - EfficientNetB2 accelerated 2.4x and 1.9x times with 0.36% and no accuracy loss, respectively. 
    - ResNeST50 is accelerated 1.5x with 0.14% accuracy drop.

Note that this is best seen in the top right figure in Table 2.


> 2. the knowledge distillation process is used for each layer separately, without considering the relation between layers. Ablation study is desired to show the advantages or disadvantages of this separate knowledge distillation.

Our approach requires per-layer distillation to enable Integer Linear Programming. The inter-layer relationships are accounted for in the `Candidate architecture evaluation` step where every discovered architecture is evaluated on the training set without training. Inter-layer relationships are ignored only when we compute the fitness metric (vector `a` in equation 3.), but during `candidate architecture evaluation`, these relationships are accounted for.   

> The comparisons in Table 2 are unfair. If we instead compare between models of the same family, no good results are obtained. For example, 0.55xEfficientB2 performs worse than the original EfficientB2. This result does not match the main idea of the paper.

Note that this is a fair comparison as we group models by their latency, please see above. With the correction of the typo, the model `0.55xEfficientNetB2` now even outperforms the original model. Please also check other important results we highlighted above. We believe the results highlighted above emphasize the main idea of the paper. 

We do hope that our strong empirical evidence can convince you that our proposed model is effective at accelerating a family of networks. We will appreciate it if you could revise your rating.

content.title: Message from authors
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and ACs, 

We would like to reiterate on the main technical novelties and empirical significance of the paper:

**Technical novelty:**

-  This paper is the first to formulate and apply Integer Linear Programming (ILP) for architecture search in the setting of network acceleration. We enable ILP by first pretraining and then scoring candidate operators. A diverse set of architectures that are constrained by budget can be found in a few seconds to minutes (large number of architectures). 
- We operate on the layer granularity and, therefore, automatically search for the depth.
- ILP allows us to operate on a significantly larger search space than previous approaches.  
- Zero-shot formulation finds architectures in few seconds with no pretraining or initialization costs. 
- Teacher-student formulation enables acceleration of existing networks and is not limited to specific architecture design. 

**Empirical significance and novelty:**

- We analyze 3 network architectures: EfficientNetV1, EfficientNetV2 and ResNeST. 
- For all the considered models, we achieve 0.18-3.0% accuracy improvement when compressing larger models to the latency level of smaller models (see EfficientNetsV1 B2->B0, B4->B2 etc). (Top right figure in Table 2).
- HANT achieves significant real speed-ups with little to no accuracy drop (Table 2): 
    - EfficeintNetB6 acceleerated by 3.6x and 1.8x times by trading-off 0.34% and 0.11% accuracy, respectively. 
    - EfficientNetB2 accelerated 2.4x and 1.9x times with 0.36% and no accuracy loss, respectively. 
    - ResNeST50 is accelerated 1.5x with 0.14% accuracy drop.
- We empirically validate the ILP metrics and solutions. Chosen objective for ILP has high correlation with the model accuracy. HANT ranks architectures before even fine tuning with the correlation of 0.85 (Figure 2, Table 3).
- We provide insights into architecture changes of all models. Section 3.2.1. Accelerated EfficientNetV1 models outperform EfficientNetV2 models specifically designed for high-throughput on GPUs. 
- Finally we validate that the obtained improvements come from the discovered architectures and not from the finetuning or knowledge distillation primarily (Table 6).

**With the help of reviewers we improved our paper:**

- Found a typo in the reported EfficientNetV1-B2 accuracy (80.39 -> 80.07). 
- Performed ablation on the search space size, and observed the improvement.
- Added results of HANT for Jetson Nano mobile platform.
- Studied the impact of finetuning length, and found that even 25 epochs is enough.
- Decided to rename the paper to Latency Aware Network Acceleration.

content.title: withdraw
content.comment: Dear reviewers and AC, we would like to thank you for your time and efforts in reading the paper and providing feedback. Given the lack of discussion, critical misunderstandings in the reviews and very limited suggestions for improvement, we have decided to withdraw the paper.
